danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 15
paragraphs: Rostov, med sin skarpe sportsmands øje, var en af de første, der fik øje på de blå franske dragoner, der forfulgte vore uhlaner. Nærmere og nærmere i uordnede klynger kom uhlanerne og de franske dragoner, der forfulgte dem. Han kunne allerede se, hvordan disse mænd, der så så små ud ved foden af bakken, stødtes og overhalede hinanden, mens de viftede med armene og sablerne i luften.

Rostov betragtede, hvad der skete foran ham, som på en jagt. Han følte instinktivt, at hvis husarerne angreb de franske dragoner nu, ville disse ikke kunne modstå dem, men hvis angrebet skulle gennemføres, måtte det ske nu, i dette øjeblik, ellers ville det være for sent. Han så sig om. En ritmester, der stod ved hans side, stirrede ligesom han med blikket rettet mod kavaleriet nedenfor.
»Andrej Sevastyánitj!« sagde Rostov. »Ved De, vi kunne knuse dem...«
»Det ville sandelig være noget!« svarede ritmesteren, »og virkelig...«

Rostov ventede ikke på, at han talte færdig, satte hælene i hesten, galoperede frem til spidsen af sin eskadron, og før han havde nået at give kommandoen til ende, fulgte hele eskadronen ham og delte hans følelse. Rostov selv vidste ikke, hvordan eller hvorfor han gjorde det. Han handlede, som han gjorde på jagt, uden at reflektere eller overveje. Han så dragonerne tæt på og i uorden; han vidste, de ikke kunne modstå et angreb — vidste, at der kun var dette ene øjeblik, og at det aldrig ville vende tilbage, hvis han lod det gå. Kuglerne peb og fløjtede så stimulerende omkring ham, og hans hest var så ivrig, at han ikke kunne holde sig tilbage. Han satte hælene i hesten, gav kommandoen, og straks, med lyden af hans deployerede eskadrons hovslag bag sig, red han i fuld trav ned ad bakken mod dragonerne. Knap havde de nået bunden af bakken, før tempoet af sig selv gik over i galop, der blev hurtigere og hurtigere, efterhånden som de nærmede sig vore uhlaner og de franske dragoner, der galoperede efter dem. Dragonerne var nu tæt på. De forreste begyndte at vende, mens de bageste begyndte at standse. Med den samme følelse, som når han galoperede tværs over en ulvs vej, gav Rostov sin Don-hest frit løb og galoperede hen for at skære vejen for dragonernes uordnede linjer. Én uhlan standsede, en anden der var til fods kastede sig til jorden for at undgå at blive væltet, og en riderløs hest faldt ind mellem husarerne. Næsten alle de franske dragoner galoperede tilbage. Rostov, der udvalgte sig en på en grå hest, satte efter ham. Undervejs stødte han på en busk, hans prægtige hest sprang over den, og næsten før han havde rettet sig i sadlen, så han, at han straks ville indhente den fjende, han havde udvalgt sig. Franskmanden, efter sin uniform at dømme en officer, red i galop, krumbøjet over sin grå hest og drev den frem med sablen. I næste øjeblik sprængte Rostovs hest brystet mod den franske officers hests bagparti og væltede den næsten, og i samme sekund løftede Rostov, uden at vide hvorfor, sablen og huggede til franskmanden.

I det øjeblik han havde gjort det, forsvandt al Rostovs livlighed. Officeren faldt, ikke så meget af hugget — der kun havde ridset hans arm over albuen — som af chokket for hesten og af skræk. Rostov holdt sin hest an, og hans øjne søgte sin fjende for at se, hvem han havde besejret. Den franske dragonofficer hoppede på den ene fod på jorden, den anden sad fast i stigbøjlen. Hans øjne, sammenknebne af frygt, som om han hvert øjeblik ventede endnu et hug, stirrede op på Rostov med krympende rædsel. Hans blege og mudderplettede ansigt — lyst og ungt, med en smule i hagen og lyseblå øjne — var slet ikke et fjendeansigt, der passede til en slagmark, men et ganske almindeligt, hjemligt ansigt. Inden Rostov havde afgjort, hvad han skulle gøre med ham, råbte officeren: »Jeg overgiver mig!« Han forsøgte hastigt men forgæves at få foden ud af stigbøjlen og fjernede ikke sine forskræmte blå øjne fra Rostovs ansigt. Nogle husarer, der galoperede til, fik hans fod fri og hjalp ham op i sadlen. På alle sider var husarerne travlt beskæftiget med dragonerne; én var såret, men selv om blodet strømmede fra hans ansigt, ville han ikke opgive sin hest; en anden sad op bag en husar med armene om ham; en tredje blev hjulpet op af en husar. Foran skød det franske infanteri, mens de løb. Husarerne galoperede hastigt tilbage med deres fanger. Rostov galoperede med de andre, bevidst om en ubehagelig følelse af nedtrykthed i sit hjerte. Noget ubestemt og forvirret, som han slet ikke kunne forklare sig, var gået over ham med tilfangetagelsen af officeren og det hug, han havde givet ham.

Grev Ostermann-Tolstój mødte de hjemvendende husarer, sendte bud efter Rostov, takkede ham og sagde, at han ville indberette hans tapre dåd til kejseren og anbefale ham til Sankt Georgs-korset. Da man sendte bud efter Rostov hos grev Ostermann, huskede han, at han havde angrebet uden ordre, og var sikker på, at hans overordnede sendte bud efter ham for at straffe ham for brud på disciplinen. Ostermanns smigrende ord og løfte om belønning burde derfor have ramt ham des behageligere, men han følte stadig den samme vagt ubehagelige følelse af moralsk kvalme. »Men hvad i alverden er det, der bekymrer mig?« spurgte han sig selv, da han red tilbage fra generalen. »Iljín? Nej, han er i sikkerhed. Har jeg vanæret mig på nogen måde? Nej, det er det ikke.« Noget andet, der lignede samvittighedsnag, plagede ham. »Ja, åh ja, den franske officer med smulen i hagen. Og jeg husker, hvordan min arm standsede, da jeg løftede den.«

Rostov så fangerne blive ført bort og galoperede efter dem for at se sin franskmand med smulen i hagen. Han sad i sin udenlandske uniform på en husarpakvogn og så sig ængsteligt om. Sabelridset på armen kunne knap kaldes et sår. Han skottede til Rostov med et påtaget smil og vinkede hilsende med hånden. Rostov følte stadig den samme ubestemte følelse af skam.

Hele den dag og den næste lagde hans venner og kammerater mærke til, at Rostov — uden at være mut eller vred — var tavs, tankefuld og indesluttet. Han drak modstræbende, forsøgte at være alene og gik stadig og vendte noget i sit sind.

Rostov tænkte uophørligt på den strålende bedrift, der til hans forbavselse havde indbragt ham Sankt Georgs-korset og endda givet ham ry for tapperhed, og der var noget, han slet ikke kunne forstå. »Så andre er endnu mere bange end jeg!« tænkte han. »Så det er alt, der er i det, man kalder heltemod! Og gjorde jeg det for fædrelandets skyld? Og hvad kunne han gøre for det, med sin smule og sine blå øjne? Hvor bange han var! Han troede, jeg ville slå ham ihjel. Hvorfor skulle jeg slå ham ihjel? Min hånd rystede. Og de har givet mig Sankt Georgs-korset... Jeg kan slet ikke finde ud af det.«

Men mens Nikolaj overvejede disse spørgsmål og stadig ikke nåede nogen klar løsning på det, der forvirrede ham, drejede lykkens hjul i tjenesten, som det ofte sker, til hans fordel. Efter affæren ved Ostróvna blev han bemærket, fik kommando over en husarbataljon, og når der var brug for en modig officer, blev han valgt.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Rostov, with his keen sportsman's eye, was one of the first to spot the blue French dragoons chasing the Russian Uhlans. Nearer and nearer, in disorderly crowds, came the Uhlans and the French dragoons pursuing them. He could already see how these men, who looked so small at the foot of the hill, were jostling and overtaking one another, waving their arms and sabers in the air.

Rostov watched what was happening before him as if at a hunt. He felt instinctively that if the hussars struck at the French dragoons now, the dragoons couldn't withstand them, but the charge had to happen immediately — at that very moment — or it would be too late. He looked around. A captain standing beside him was staring like himself with eyes fixed on the cavalry below.
"Andrew Sevastyanych!" said Rostov. "You know, we could crush them..."
"A fine thing too!" replied the captain, "and really..."

Rostov, without waiting to hear him out, spurred his horse, galloped to the front of his squadron, and before he had time to finish giving the word of command, the whole squadron, sharing his instinct, was following him. Rostov himself didn't know how or why he did it. He acted as he did when hunting — without reflecting or thinking. He saw the dragoons near and disordered; he knew they couldn't withstand an attack — knew there was only this one moment, and that if he let it pass it wouldn't return. The bullets were whining and whistling so stimulatingly around him and his horse was so eager to go that he couldn't hold back. He spurred his horse, gave the word of command, and immediately, hearing behind him the thundering hooves of his deployed squadron, rode at full trot downhill toward the dragoons. Hardly had they reached the bottom of the hill before their pace instinctively changed to a gallop, which grew faster and faster as they drew nearer to the Uhlans and the French dragoons galloping after them. The dragoons were now close at hand. On seeing the hussars, those in front began to turn while those behind started to pull up. With the same feeling with which he had galloped to cut off a wolf, Rostov gave full rein to his Don horse and galloped to intersect the path of the dragoons' disordered lines. One Uhlan stopped, another who was on foot flung himself to the ground to avoid being knocked over, and a riderless horse fell in among the hussars. Nearly all the French dragoons were galloping back. Rostov, picking out one on a gray horse, dashed after him. On the way he came to a bush; his gallant horse cleared it, and almost before he had righted himself in the saddle he saw that he would immediately overtake the enemy he had singled out. That Frenchman, by his uniform an officer, was going at a gallop, crouching on his gray horse and urging it on with his saber. In another instant Rostov's horse dashed its chest against the hindquarters of the officer's horse, almost knocking it over, and at the same instant Rostov, without knowing why, raised his saber and struck the Frenchman with it.

The instant he had done this, all Rostov's excitement vanished. The officer fell — not so much from the blow, which had only slightly cut his arm above the elbow, as from the shock to his horse and from fright. Rostov reined in his horse and his eyes sought his foe to see whom he had conquered. The French dragoon officer was hopping with one foot on the ground, the other caught in the stirrup. His eyes, screwed up with fear as if he expected another blow at any moment, gazed up at Rostov with shrinking terror. His pale and mud-stained face — fair and young, with a dimple in the chin and light blue eyes — was not an enemy's face at all suited to a battlefield, but a perfectly ordinary, domestic face. Before Rostov had decided what to do with him, the officer cried: "I surrender!" He hurriedly but vainly tried to free his foot from the stirrup and didn't take his frightened blue eyes from Rostov's face. Some hussars who galloped up freed his foot and helped him into the saddle. On all sides the hussars were busy with the dragoons; one was wounded, but though his face was bleeding he wouldn't give up his horse; another was perched behind a hussar with his arms around him; a third was being helped by a hussar to mount. In front, the French infantry were firing as they ran. The hussars galloped hastily back with their prisoners. Rostov galloped back with the rest, aware of an unpleasant feeling of heaviness in his heart. Something vague and confused, which he couldn't account for at all, had come over him with the capture of that officer and the blow he had dealt him.

Count Ostermann-Tolstoy met the returning hussars, sent for Rostov, thanked him, and said he would report his gallant deed to the Emperor and would recommend him for the St. George's Cross. When sent for by Count Ostermann, Rostov, remembering that he had charged without orders, felt sure his commander was summoning him to punish him for breach of discipline. Ostermann's flattering words and promise of a reward should therefore have pleased him all the more, but he still felt that same vaguely disagreeable sense of moral unease. "But what on earth is bothering me?" he asked himself as he rode back from the general. "Ilyin? No, he's safe. Have I disgraced myself in some way? No, that's not it." Something else, resembling remorse, tormented him. "Yes, oh yes — that French officer with the dimple. And I remember how my arm hesitated when I raised it."

Rostov saw the prisoners being led away and galloped after them to get another look at his Frenchman with the dimple on his chin. He was sitting in his foreign uniform on a hussar packhorse and looked anxiously around. The sword cut on his arm could hardly be called a wound. He glanced at Rostov with a forced smile and waved his hand in greeting. Rostov still felt the same indefinite sense of shame.

All that day and the next his friends and comrades noticed that Rostov, without being sulky or angry, was silent, thoughtful, and preoccupied. He drank reluctantly, tried to be alone, and kept turning something over in his mind.

Rostov was constantly thinking about that brilliant exploit of his, which to his amazement had earned him the St. George's Cross and even given him a reputation for bravery, and there was something he couldn't understand at all. "So others are even more afraid than I am!" he thought. "So that's all there is to what they call heroism! And did I do it for my country's sake? And how was he to blame, with his dimple and blue eyes? And how frightened he was! He thought I was going to kill him. Why should I kill him? My hand trembled. And they've given me a St. George's Cross... I can't make it out at all."

But while Nicholas was pondering these questions and still couldn't reach a clear answer to what puzzled him so, the wheel of fortune in the service, as often happens, turned in his favor. After the action at Ostrovna he was brought to notice, given command of a hussar battalion, and whenever a brave officer was needed he was chosen.
